teaser: The four-meter canvas that introduced an unknown foreigner to Toledo, signed and dated on a scrap of paper.
review_notes:
Dated 1577 on the painting; the altarpiece of Santo Domingo el Antiguo was completed and installed in 1579.
Size about 403 x 212 cm.
Commission from Diego de Castilla, dean of Toledo Cathedral, arranged through his son Luis, whom El Greco knew in Rome: standard account.
The Greek signature is usually translated roughly as 'Domenikos Theotokopoulos, Cretan, displayed this, 1577'.
The Disrobing of Christ (El Espolio) for Toledo Cathedral was commissioned in 1577, the same year.
Sold from the church about 1830 to the Infante Sebastian Gabriel de Borbon and replaced by a copy; bought by the Art Institute of Chicago in 1906 on Mary Cassatt's urging.
El Greco was buried at Santo Domingo el Antiguo in 1614; the later fate of his remains is uncertain.
No eyewitness account of the first viewers' reaction survives; the lesson says so.

lesson.text: Picture the nuns of Santo Domingo el Antiguo, a convent in Toledo, Spain, on the day in 1579 when the new altarpiece in their church was finally uncovered. In the center, more than four meters tall, a woman in blue rises off the ground on a sliver of moon. The painter is a stranger in his thirties, just arrived from Italy. Almost nobody in town has seen his work.

No one wrote down what the nuns said. But we know how Toledo answered, because the answer was work. The cathedral had not even waited for the unveiling: it ordered a major painting from the newcomer while he was still busy with this one. Churches and private patrons kept him employed for the next 37 years.

His name was Domenikos Theotokopoulos, born on the Greek island of Crete, trained in Venice, then stuck in Rome without much success. A Spanish friend there had a father who ran Toledo's cathedral and was rebuilding a convent church. That is how a Greek got the job: nine paintings, plus the design of the carved frame that held them.
This canvas was the centerpiece of the set. It is about 4 meters high and 2.1 meters wide (around 13 by 7 feet), far bigger than anything he had tried before.

The subject is the Assumption: the Catholic belief that Mary, the mother of Jesus, was taken up to heaven, body and soul, at the end of her life. The apostles, the followers of Jesus, gather at her tomb and find it empty. A story that moves straight up needs a picture built to match.
The tall canvas is stacked in two floors, joined by one rising line.

lines.label: The cloud floor
lines.text: A bank of gray cloud cuts the picture in half. Above it is heaven, crowded with angels. Below it is earth, crowded with men.

lines.label: The gap
lines.text: The apostles split into two groups and leave a V of empty air between them. It works like an open door for your eye to pass through.

lines.label: The way up
lines.text: From the stone tomb, through the gap, past the moon and along the blue robe to Mary's lifted face: a single path, bottom to top.

lesson.text: El Greco did not invent this two-floor design. Sixty years earlier Titian, the great master of Venice, had painted a giant Assumption for a church there, and every young painter in the city studied it. The newcomer was telling Toledo where he came from. He was also telling them who he was, in a spot that is easy to miss.
The painter signed and dated this picture on a small piece of paper painted into the scene. Where is it?

spots.title: The paper note
spots.text: A creased white slip seems stuck to the picture near an apostle's staff. On it, in Greek letters, he gives his full name, calls himself a Cretan, and adds the year: 1577.

lesson.text: A fake piece of paper that looks pinned to the surface is a trick Venetian painters loved. Writing on it in Greek, in the middle of Spain, was his own idea. He signed that way for the rest of his life, and the Spaniards met him halfway: they simply called him El Greco, “the Greek.”
This is El Greco's entrance exam, and he passes it by showing everything he learned in Italy at once: Venetian color, a famous composition, and bodies with real weight.

Those bodies matter. If you know his later work, with its thin, flame-like figures, these people may surprise you. Their arms are thick, their feet are planted, their robes hang heavy. The stretching has barely begun. What is already his is the color: sharp pink, cold blue, acid yellow, set side by side with no soft browns in between.

lesson.title: Three ways to react
lesson.text: Go from the sky down to the ground. Each stop shows a different response to the same event.

spots.title: Mary
spots.text: Arms flung wide, eyes turned up, she does not look back at the ground. Her red sleeves and blue cloak are the strongest colors in the upper half.

spots.title: The crescent moon
spots.text: Her feet rest on a thin white moon, an old symbol of her purity. It sits exactly on the border between the two halves, like a hinge.

spots.title: The man from behind
spots.text: A big apostle in yellow and pink turns his back to you and holds out a hand. You stand just behind him, so you look where he looks.

spots.title: Still looking down
spots.text: On the right, a bald apostle and an old man in blue bend toward the tomb. They have not understood yet. The answer is above their heads.

lesson.text: Some of the men look up, some look at each other, some keep searching the empty stone box. It is a small study of how news travels through a crowd. And by placing that broad back at the front, El Greco gives you a role too: one more witness at the edge of the group.

The nuns sold the painting around 1830 and hung a copy in its place, which is still there. The original reached Chicago in 1906 after the American painter Mary Cassatt saw it in Europe and urged the Art Institute to buy it.

The rest of the altarpiece was scattered too. The scene that sat directly above this one, showing God the Father holding the dead Christ, is now in the Prado museum in Madrid. To see the set as the nuns did, you would have to visit several cities and put it back together in your head.
El Greco stayed loyal to the church that gave him his start. When he died in Toledo in 1614, he was buried at Santo Domingo el Antiguo, a few steps from the frame he had designed 37 years earlier.

quiz.question: How did Toledo respond to the newcomer's altarpiece?
options: With new orders, starting with the cathedral
The painting was hidden for decades
quiz.explanation: The cathedral hired him before this job was even finished, and work kept coming for 37 years.

quiz.question: Whose earlier Assumption inspired the two-floor design?
quiz.explanation: Titian's giant Assumption in Venice was studied by every young painter there.

quiz.question: What is written on the painted slip of paper?
options: The painter's name in Greek letters and the year 1577
quiz.explanation: He signs in Greek, calls himself a Cretan and gives the date.

quiz.question: What does Mary stand on?
quiz.explanation: A thin white moon, a symbol of her purity, sits under her feet.

quiz.question: Who urged the Art Institute of Chicago to buy the painting?
quiz.explanation: Cassatt saw it in Europe and pushed for the 1906 purchase.

quiz.question: How do the figures here differ from El Greco's later ones?
options: They are tiny and far away
They are solid and heavy, not yet stretched thin
quiz.explanation: The thick arms and planted feet show his elongated style has barely begun.

facts.text: El Greco signed this painting in Greek letters.
facts.explanation: The slip of paper at the lower right carries his Greek name and the year 1577.

facts.text: The original canvas still hangs in the convent church in Toledo.
facts.explanation: The nuns sold it around 1830; a copy hangs there, and the original is in Chicago.

facts.text: All the apostles in the picture are looking up at Mary.
facts.explanation: Several still bend toward the empty tomb or look at each other.
